title: Satie: from piano to six strings
question: How does a guitar keep Satie’s melody singing above the bass and chords?
intro: Satie’s first Gymnopédie begins with four bars of bass notes and chords, swaying in three beats. Then a melody enters, hanging above the accompaniment. Robin Alciatore plays the piano original; Michael Laucke fits all three parts onto six guitar strings.

recordings.label: Robin Alciatore
recordings.note: Alciatore plays Satie’s original solo-piano version in this recording released through Musopen.

recordings.label: Michael Laucke
recordings.note: Laucke plays his own arrangement on one classical guitar, without overdubbing.

passages.label: The melody enters
passages.note: The melody steps into the space above the bass and chords; its longer notes stretch across the three-beat accompaniment.

passages.label: The melody drops
passages.note: The piano melody settles on a low E, held while the bass and chords change beneath it.

passages.label: Four bars before the tune
passages.note: The opening bass notes and chords return alone. Four bars pass before the melody joins them again.

passages.label: The changed ending
passages.note: In the piano score, F♮ replaces F♯, and the melody’s rising C♯–D–E becomes falling E–D–C.

passages.label: The final minor chord
passages.note: The piano closes on D minor: F♮ sits between D and A, and the last chord hangs in the air.
